56 MATCHES 01 / 05

30 days. One player. No data.

I played Hitwicket for 30 days.

56 matches. 64% win rate. I still had no reason to open it tomorrow.

Funny how I think saying what makes Hitwicket bad will get me a job — Abhinav Pentani

Scroll
Not an application. Not a case study I was given. I played the game, wrote down what broke, and tried to work out why.
The five things

Five problems, in the order I hit them.

01I expected a different game→ 02I didn't know what I was playing toward→ 03My alliance had 30 members and none of them mattered→ 04The home screen gives me 15 things to do→ 05By match 40, every match felt like the last one→

Problem 3 is the one I think matters most. The rest either lead into it or fall out of it.

The fix →
01 / 05

I expected a different game.

Anecdote

The Play Store said “multiplayer cricket game.” Then: “play as an owner, coach and captain of your own cricket team.” I expected Real Cricket. WCC. Something where I bat.

Then my first match loaded.

Five numbers and five percentages.
I didn't know what set the percentages, what they were relative to, or why one number was better than another.
I uninstalled after that match.

The problem

I reinstalled. It took me until somewhere around match 15 to 20 to understand that each run is tied to a shot type, that the shot should match the ball being bowled, and that 0s, 1s and 2s build a superpower meter you spend later. (Maybe I'm dumb enough not to notice this earlier. So are a lot of our users.)

That is a good cricketing idea. Build the innings, then attack. The game just never told me. Spoiler: the tutorial optimised for explaining features, not the core loop.

But the comprehension gap is the smaller half of this.
Once I understood the mechanic, my actual decision was still: pick the run I want, look at the percentage, tap.
I almost never reasoned about the ball, the shot, or the bowler's ability. Understanding the system did not change how I played it.

Harsha Bhogle, on a real match:

“A spinner is bowling, you lose a wicket on the first ball of the over, would you promote your exceptional spin-hitter up the order knowing that the 5 balls left in the over constitute 4% of the match? Because that's exactly what CSK did the other day.”

That is the decision I want to be making. That is a state I am reading and a counter-decision I am taking.
I never once felt that in 56 matches.

Confirmation

I checked whether this was just me.

The first match is a comprehension problem. Every match after it is a depth problem.

Teaching players why 0s and 1s matter could reduce first-session drop-off. But once understood, the mechanic still feels shallow: the interface makes probability the decision, rather than the game state.

And while removing percentages may make the game harder to process, the bigger issue is that the UI doesn't clearly show what those percentages are actually based on: the relationship between the ball, the shot and the bowler.

Leads to

Two fixes, at two different depths.

PS: I know the design looks really bad. Maybe we'll work something out once I join you guys, lol.

The deeper fix is not a UI change. It is making the bowler's choice visible enough that my choice becomes a response to it rather than a selection from a menu. I have flagged that as a direction, not a design. I don't have the data to design it.

 Next: I didn't know what I was playing toward →
02 / 05

I didn't know what I was playing toward.

Anecdote

Around match 30, a friend asked me what I was trying to do in the game.
I couldn't answer in one sentence.

8/67
players scouted after 30 days
11/56
of my matches were Tour matches
0
achievements, in 56 matches
The problem

Every game I have put real time into gave me one thing to chase.

Hitwicket has a season pass, achievements, XP, scout points, tiers and alliance levels. Six small things to run behind. Nothing concrete.

I wasn't avoiding these systems. They just never became the thing.

Confirmation

Hitwicket has many progression systems and no single visible objective, so effort does not accumulate into anything a player can name.

A player who cannot state what they are chasing in one sentence has no reason to return on a day they don't feel like playing.

Leads to

I don't think the fix is a seventh progression system.
I think the thing worth chasing in a mid-core game usually isn't individual. Which is where the next problem starts.

PS: I think we can figure something out for this together once I join your team, hehe.

← PreviousNext: the alliance →
03 / 05Primary argument

My alliance had 30 members and none of them mattered.

Anecdote

I am in an alliance called “The top players alliance.” Kind of ironic, given the name.
I have never once opened Hitwicket because of it.

30/30
members
0
online
0
alliance trophies, after 30 days
The problem

The alliance is not missing. The infrastructure is all there.

Chat. Requests. Help. Boosting. An Academy. Squad Rush. Roles.
All of it is a feature. None of it is a loop.

The game does show flashes of the right thing. “Your alliance has boosted Phoenix to level 1.” “2 people have helped.” Action, then visible shared progress. The mechanism exists. It just isn't attached to anything I care about winning.

The question I could never answer:

What am I supposed to come back tomorrow to accomplish with these 29 people?

I also asked three friends to install and play for twenty minutes, then asked them one question: would anything make you open this again tomorrow?

The part that isn't about me

Keerti has said publicly that we're on a journey from 100,000 DAU to 1M. I don't see how that happens without peer-to-peer onboarding: friends bringing friends, playing in teams. Kashyap has talked about UA as the primary growth lever.

I got to the same layer from the other direction, as a player.

My worry is the sequence. Friends will not onboard friends into an alliance where 30 of 30 members are offline. A viral loop needs a working social loop underneath it.

Hitwicket has the infrastructure for social play, but because the alliance has no simple, visible, time-bound shared objective, it behaves as a collection of utilities rather than a team.

If an alliance is given a shared objective that visibly depends on individual contribution, the return trigger moves from personal motivation to social obligation.

Obligation to a named group is a stronger reason to open an app than a reminder from one.

Leads to

Attach the match I already play to a time-bound alliance-vs-alliance objective, so that one player's match creates a visible collective consequence.
No new currency. No new game mode. No change to monetisation. The match stays exactly as it is.

04 / 05

The home screen gives me 15 things to do.

Minor. Friction, not thesis.
Anecdote

I opened the app knowing I wanted to play a match. It still took me a moment to find where.

The problem

Almost everything in the game is reachable from here, which means nothing on the screen is emphasised.

This is minor on its own. It matters because it sits on top of Problem 2. If a player already doesn't know what they're chasing, a screen with fifteen equal paths doesn't help them pick one.

The home screen optimises for access, not for the next action.

A player who arrives without a clear goal leaves without taking one.

Leads to

Ugh, something like this. Need to work on the design again, lol.

← PreviousNext: variability →
05 / 05

By match 40, every match felt like the last one.

Secondary. A thread I'd want to pull, not a conclusion I've reached.
Anecdote

I love cricket enough that I kept playing. That is why I got to 56 matches and 64%.
It is also why I noticed that match 45 and match 12 were not meaningfully different experiences.

The problem

Cricket is inherently repetitive. Every sport game has to solve this. Most solve it by changing the frame rather than the sport.

Season passes are the usual answer, and I'm not convinced they work here.
A pass rewards playing more. But if the reason to play more is weak, the pass is asking me to commit to something I'm not already pulled toward. That looks like a cold start.
I want to flag that as a question rather than assert it. I can't see the pass conversion data.

Variability across matches, not reward volume, is what keeps a repetitive sport loop alive.

Two matches should be able to feel different because the conditions were different, not because the rewards were.

Leads to

Directions rather than a design, because I don't have enough to design here:

Conditions that change the correct strategy, not the payout. Pitch behaviour, weather, chase targets, restricted squads.

AI commentary that reacts to the specific state, so the same scoreline reads differently depending on how you got there.

A rotating constraint per cycle that forces a different lineup.

Bad design, but it already feels like more strategy is involved.

The Fix→

The fix

The Fix

Attach the match I already play to a time-bound alliance-vs-alliance objective, so that one player's match creates a visible collective consequence.

No new currency. No new game mode. No change to monetisation. The match stays exactly as it is.
The fixture

The fixture is the shared goal. The notification at the midpoint turns it into my responsibility.

Why this and not something else
The experiment
Primary metricD14 return rate of alliance members: openings on days they didn't plan to play.
ComparisonAlliance as shipped today: chat, requests, help, boosting, Academy, Squad Rush. No fixture.
Randomise onAlliance, not player. A social mechanic leaks across a player-level split, and the control group stops being a control.
SecondaryFixture-notification open rate, and matches started inside the fixture window.
GuardrailMatch length and pace. If players rush matches to farm contribution, the game got worse while the metric improved.
Bar to roll widerA significant lift on the primary metric, no guardrail breach, held across two fixture cycles.

One variable. The match itself does not change.

What I don't know

Most of what I've written rests on one player's 30 days. These are the things I'd need your data to answer, and any of them could change the conclusion.

  • Do alliance members already retain better than non-members? If they do, this is an amplifier, not a fix, and the case for building it is different.
  • What share of players ever join an alliance at all? If it's small, discovery is the problem and the fixture solves nothing.
  • Is Squad Rush under-used or under-found? I couldn't tell from the outside, and the answer points to two different fixes.
  • Is my first-match confusion typical? My D1 experience is one sample. Your funnel knows.
  • What does the season pass actually convert at? My cold-start argument depends on a number I don't have.

About Abhinav Pentani

Why this exists

Why this exists.

I applied to Hitwicket about a month ago and was rejected. No feedback, and I understand why: a resume is a thin thing to judge on.

So I played the game for 30 days instead, and wrote down what I found. This is the only thing I can show you that a resume can't. Kashyap has written that gaming is one of the hardest product disciplines there is: economies, player psychology, retention curves, live ops, competitive depth, all at once. I agree, and that is exactly why I want to work on it. This is my attempt at doing a small part of it from the outside, with none of the data and all of the guesswork that implies.

Who I am

Abhinav Pentani. Hyderabad. Final-year CS at VIT-AP.

I currently work as a Product Analyst at Alfaleus Technology, a medical device startup, where I work on usage and clinical feedback data and turn it into product changes. Before that I co-founded Vectr, a content-tech venture, where I ran growth and took it to 10,000+ installs and 3,000+ pre-registrations. I've also spent time as a Venture Analyst screening 100+ early-stage companies. Rank 16 of 800+ colleges at IIT Bombay's National Entrepreneurship Challenge. Runner-up of 900+ teams at the Proxy National Hackathon.

Selected Project
Hitwicket Retention Analysis2026
Self-initiated funnel and retention teardown of a live mobile game
  • Ran a 30-day, 56-match cohort-of-one study and mapped drop points across the full funnel: install expectation mismatch at D0, comprehension failure in the first session, fragmented progression by week two, no social trigger by week four.
  • Identified the retention gap as between-session, not in-session: engagement while playing was strong, but no mechanism outside the app created a reason to reopen it.
  • Argued that peer-to-peer acquisition, the stated path from 100K to 1M DAU, is gated on a functioning social retention loop, since users will not invite friends into alliances where 30 of 30 members are inactive.
  • Designed a testable intervention and specified measurement: return rate as primary, notification open rate and in-window matches as secondary, match length and pace as a guardrail, randomized at alliance level to prevent leakage across a social mechanic.
  • Documented the internal metrics that would falsify the hypothesis, including baseline alliance-member retention and alliance join rate.
